# DDAR Exercise 1.1
## a) *"Examine a number of recent issues of a scientific or statistical journal in which you have some interest. Find one or more examples of a graph or table that is a particularly bad use of display material to summarize and communicate research findings. Write a few sentences indicating how or why the display fails and how it could be improved."*

```{r echo=FALSE, out.width = "450pt", out.height = "304.5pt", fig.align = "center"}
knitr::include_graphics("/Users/gklorfine/Desktop/School/Graduate/MA/Winter 2026/PSYC6136 Categorical/6136catego/images/badgraph.jpg")
```

Retrieved from: https://doi.org/10.1155/2022/3802603

This graph is from a (now retracted) paper that was published in *Advances in Materials Science and Engineering* 
in 2022. It attempts to depict the selectivity of a biosensor with several 
enzymes interfering. From the text, it is not clear what this graph attempts to 
show and why "pink" deviates from the rest of the enzymes. Additionally, "pink" 
and "blank" are not enzymes. An *x*-axis label would help to clear the 
confusion regarding "pink" and "blank." Furthermore, the "error bars" are 
actually the letter "T" superimposed on the graph. Authors should have used a 
statistical measure of uncertainty (e.g., standard error) to construct proper 
error bars. Last, the graph would benefit from a title and a better explanation 
in the figure caption (as is, the caption simply reads "Selectivity of the 
analytical method.").


# DDAR Exercise 1.2
## *"As in the previous exercise, examine the recent literature in recent issues of some journal of interest to you. Find one or more examples of a graph or table that you feel does a good job of summarizing and communicating research findings."*

```{r echo=FALSE, out.width = "379pt", out.height = "320pt", fig.align = "center"}
knitr::include_graphics("/Users/gklorfine/Desktop/School/Graduate/MA/Winter 2026/PSYC6136 Categorical/6136catego/images/goodgraph.png")
```

Retrieved from: https://doi.org/10.1037/neu0001058

## a) *"Write a few sentences describing why you chose these displays."*

This graph published in *Neuropsychology* in 2025 shows how a participant's
ability to recall a word changes depending on both the position of the word in a
list and whether the language was his/her dominant or non-dominant. From the
graph, primacy and recency effects on recall are indicated through the higher
recall proportion for the first few and last few words in the list, with the
minimum recall proportion being located near the middle of the list. We may
also see that recall proportion is higher if the words were in the participant's
dominant language. A proper title and axes labels were included.

## b) *"Now take the role of a tough journal reviewer. Are there any features of the display that could be modified to make them more effective?"*

This graph can be modified to directly label the dominant and non-dominant 
curves with text, as opposed to the inclusion of a legend. It might also
benefit from a figure caption to assist the reader in quickly understanding
the information conveyed.

# DDAR Exercise 2.2
## *"For each of the following data sets in the vcdExtra package, identify which are response variable(s) and which are explanatory. For factor variables, which are unordered (nominal) and which should be treated as ordered? Write a sentence or two describing substantitive questions of interest for analysis of the data. (Hint: use `data(foo, package="vcdExtra")` to load, and `str(foo)`, `help(foo)` to examine data set `foo`.)"*

## a) *"Abortion opinion data"*

```{r abortion}
data(Abortion, package="vcdExtra")
?vcdExtra::Abortion
```
1. `Support_Abortion` is a nominal response variable
1. `Status` is an ordinal explanatory variable
1. `Sex` is a nominal explanatory variable

Do sex and/or status meaningfully predict whether one supports abortion?

## b) *"Caesarian births data"*

```{r Caesarian}
data(Caesar, package="vcdExtra")
?vcdExtra::Caesar
```
1. `Infection` is a response variable. If a `Type 1` infection is better/worse 
than a `Type 2` infection, `Infection` may be treated as ordered upon severity.
Else, `Infection` is nominal.
1. `Risk` is a nominal explanatory variable
1. `Antibiotics` is a nominal explanatory variable
1. `Planned` is a nominal explanatory variable

Does the presence of risk factors, being given antibiotics, and/or having 
planned the C section meaningfully predict infection absence/type?

## c) *"Dayton Survey data"*

```{r Dayton}
data("DaytonSurvey", package="vcdExtra")
?vcdExtra::DaytonSurvey
```
1. `cigarette` is a nominal response variable
1. `alcohol` is a nominal response variable
1. `marijuana` is a nominal response variable
1. `sex` is a nominal explanatory variable
1. `race` is a nominal explanatory variable

Do sex and/or race meaningfully predict whether high school seniors have ever
used alcohol, cigarettes, and/or marijuana?

## d) *"Minnesota high school graduates data"*

```{r Minn}
data(Hoyt, package="vcdExtra")
?vcdExtra::Hoyt
```
1. `Status` is a nominal response variable
1. `Rank` is an ordinal explanatory variable
1. `Occupation` is an ordinal explanatory variable
1. `Sex` is a nominal explanatory variable

Do sex, one's rank in his/her graduating class, one's father's occupational
status, and/or one's sex meaningfully predict one's post high-school status?

# DDAR Exercise 2.4
## *"The data set DanishWelfare in vcd gives a 4-way, 3 $\times$ 4 $\times$ 3 $\times$ 5 table as a data frame in frequency form, containing the variable `Freq` and four factors, `Alcohol`, `Income`, `Status` and `Urban`. The variable `Alcohol` can be considered as the response variable, and the others as possible predictors."*

## a) *"Find the total number of cases represented in this table"*

```{r a}
data("DanishWelfare", package = "vcd")
(sum(DanishWelfare$Freq))
```

## b) *"In this form, the variables `Alcohol` and `Income` should arguably be considered ordered factors. Change them to make them ordered."*

```{r b}
df <- DanishWelfare

df$Alcohol <- ordered(df$Alcohol,
                      levels = c("<1", "1-2", ">2"))
df$Income <- ordered(df$Income,
                     levels = c("0-50", "50-100", "100-150", ">150"))
```

## c) *"Convert this data frame to table form, `DanishWelfare.tab`, a 4-way array containing the frequencies with appropriate variable names and level names."*

```{r c}
DanishWelfare.tab <- with(df, xtabs(Freq ~ Alcohol + Income + Status + Urban))
structable(Alcohol ~ Income + Status + Urban, data = DanishWelfare.tab)
```

## d) *"The variable Urban has 5 categories. Find the total frequencies in each of these. How would you collapse the table to have only two categories, `City`, `Non-city`?"*

```{r d}
# Total frequencies in each Urban category
margin.table(DanishWelfare.tab, "Urban")

# Collapse Urban to two categories: City, Non-city
twoCat <- collapse.table(DanishWelfare.tab,
                         Urban = c("City", "Non-city", "City", "City", "Non-city"))
```

## e) *"Use `structable()` or `ftable()` to produce a pleasing flattened display of the frequencies in the 4-way table. Choose the variables used as row and column variables to make it easier to compare levels of `Alcohol` across the other factors."*

```{r e}
structable(Alcohol ~ Income + Status + Urban, data = twoCat)
```
